title: Daily Health Briefing
intro: Good morning! Today's digest pulls fresh, reputable research across your tracked topics — anti-aging, HIIT for women, pelvic floor training, integrative + targeted options for HER2+/TP53 breast cancer, and sleep. Sources (PubMed, JAMA Network, NIH/NHLBI, Nature, Frontiers, ClinicalTrials.gov) are linked as chips under each section. Informational only — talk to a clinician before acting on anything here.

sections.body:
This week's evidence keeps pulling in the same direction: clear *biological activity*, but still no supplement proven to slow human aging. Judge interventions by clocks and function, not marketing.

- **NAD⁺ boosters (NR/NMN).** A new PRISMA systematic review (113 studies; 33 human, 28 randomized) found oral **nicotinamide riboside** and **NMN** reliably raise NAD-related blood markers and are well tolerated over weeks to months — but effects on functional, metabolic, and vascular healthspan outcomes were **heterogeneous and often null**. Target engagement ≠ anti-aging benefit.
- **Rapamycin reality check.** The **PEARL** trial (2025) — the largest, longest RCT of intermittent low-dose rapamycin (5 or 10 mg/week for 48 weeks in healthy older adults) — found it **relatively safe**, with only *modest* gains (muscle mass and self-reported pain/well-being in women at the higher dose). A 2026 review still concludes there's **no clear clinical evidence** that rapalogs slow human aging.
- **Senolytics.** A 2026 systematic review found only ~6 completed human studies; **dasatinib + quercetin** showed preliminary functional gains and lower senescence biomarkers, but these remain **investigational, not established** therapies.
- **What actually moves next-gen epigenetic clocks.** A 2026 review of 41 human studies found **exercise, a plant-rich diet, caloric restriction, omega-3s, a multivitamin, semaglutide, and pitavastatin** decreased epigenetic age — while **NR, rapamycin, and senolytics showed no detectable effect** on those clocks. Lifestyle still leads.
- **One to watch.** The **TauAge** RCT (NCT06613542; 90 adults 55–75, 4 g/day taurine for 6 months) completed Nov 2025 with biological-age endpoints — results pending. Treat taurine as an *emerging* candidate, not a validated one.

sections.body:
New 2026 meta-analyses reinforce HIIT as a **time-efficient cardio and fat-loss tool** for women — with one consistent caveat: it won't build strength on its own, so **pair it with resistance training**.

- **Middle-aged & older women.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Physiology* review (19 RCTs, 646 women) found HIIT **strongly improves VO₂max** (SMD 1.20, high certainty) but had **no significant effect on muscle strength, flexibility, or sit-to-stand**, with only borderline walking gains. Conclusion: HIIT alone is insufficient for overall functional fitness.
- **Overweight/obesity.** A 2026 meta-analysis (15 RCTs) showed HIIT significantly reduced **body weight, BMI, body-fat %, and fat mass**, raised VO₂max (Hedges' g 1.09), increased HDL and lowered LDL — though total cholesterol and triglyceride effects were not significant (low certainty). Expect **recomposition more than big scale drops**.
- **Postmenopausal women.** A network meta-analysis (51 RCTs, ~2,046 women) ranked **HIIT the most efficacious** exercise for lowering **triglycerides**, with a *non-linear* dose-response — benefits plateaued around **1,000–1,300 MET-min/week**. More isn't always better; aim for an effective dose and recover well.

Bottom line: 2–3 HIIT sessions/week for cardio and fat loss, **plus strength work** for the muscle, bone, and functional gains HIIT doesn't deliver alone.

sections.body:
**Pelvic floor muscle training (PFMT)** stays the first-line, evidence-based treatment for stress urinary incontinence (SUI). The newest 2026 trials sharpen *how* to do it well and *what* to add.

- **PFMT beats Pilates.** A 2026 RCT (*Int Urogynecol J*) of 12 supervised sessions over 6 weeks found **targeted PFMT** cut incontinence impact (ICIQ-SF) by **−4.4 points vs −0.7** for Pilates (±voluntary contraction), with far larger gains in muscle strength and vaginal squeeze pressure. General core work is **not** a substitute for isolated pelvic-floor training.
- **Add biofeedback (for symptoms) or radiofrequency (for sexual function).** A 2026 RCT (45 women) found all groups improved, but **PFMT + biofeedback** gave the biggest gains in muscle strength, endurance, and incontinence symptoms, while **PFMT + radiofrequency** most improved sexual function (FSFI). Biofeedback helps confirm you're activating the right muscles.
- **Prevention works in pregnancy.** A multicenter JAMA Network Open RCT (**PEFLOW**, 764 first-time mothers) found in-pregnancy pelvic-floor training lowered postpartum SUI at 6 weeks to **8.7% vs 13.9%**, with more women reaching strong pelvic-floor scores.

Key point: **technique and consistency beat raw reps.** A typical starting prescription is 10 contractions (building toward 8–10 s holds) × ~3 sets daily; confirm correct activation with a clinician or biofeedback.

sections.topic: Alternative & Integrative + Targeted Options — HER2+ / TP53 Breast Cancer
sections.body:
Read "alternative" as **evidence-based integrative care alongside standard treatment** — not a replacement. The most actionable 2026 news for HER2+/TP53-altered disease is on the *targeted* side.

- **Supplements: mechanism ≠ proof.** A 2026 *review of natural supplements in breast cancer* (curcumin, withaferin A, luteolin, quercetin, resveratrol) found mostly **preclinical/early-phase** signals, limited by poor bioavailability, non-standardized products, and real **herb–drug interaction** risk. Use only within evidence-based practice and **coordinate with your oncology team** — some can blunt or amplify targeted therapy.
- **TP53 mutation = a targetable vulnerability.** New preclinical work shows that in **HER2-mutant tumors, co-occurring TP53 mutations drive resistance to neratinib but heightened sensitivity to T-DXd** (the TOP1-inhibitor payload in trastuzumab deruxtecan), via histone-acetylation-driven chromatin accessibility. The **neratinib + T-DXd** combination is now in a phase I trial (NCT05372614).
- **First targetable p53 alteration.** For the specific **TP53 Y220C** mutation, the p53 reactivator **rezatapopt** is in the pivotal phase 2 **PYNNACLE** basket trial (NCT04585750) that *includes a breast cohort*; interim gynecologic data showed meaningful responses (ovarian ORR ~44–46%). Note Y220C is **rare in HER2+** disease, so genomic testing matters to know if it applies.

Important framing: much integrative evidence is early/observational. Use supplements as **adjuncts discussed with an oncologist**, never as substitutes for HER2-targeted therapy.

sections.topic: Sleep — Fragmented/Restless Sleep: Studies & Best Practices
sections.body:
For restless or disjointed sleep, the 2026 message is unchanged and strong: **behavioral therapy first, pills and supplements second** — and use melatonin for *timing*, not as a sleeping pill.

- **CBT-I is first-line.** The 2026 *Nature Reviews Disease Primers* overview and the VA/DoD (2025) and NIH/NHLBI guidance all put **cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia (CBT-I)** ahead of medication. Its core tools — **sleep restriction, stimulus control, relaxation, and cognitive restructuring** — directly target the fragmented, wake-after-sleep-onset pattern. **Digital CBT-I** makes it widely accessible.
- **Melatonin, used correctly.** NIH notes melatonin is **not proven to treat insomnia**; it helps mainly with **circadian timing** (jet lag, delayed phase) and **sleep-onset latency**, *not* sleep maintenance or early waking. If using it to shift phase, evidence favors a **small dose (~0.5 mg) taken ~5 hours before your target sleep onset** — not the 30–60-min-before-bed label dose, which can backfire. **Skip OTC antihistamine sleep aids.**
- **Match the fix to the cause.** A 2026 *Frontiers in Psychiatry* framework highlights that some "insomnia" is really **circadian misalignment**; adjuncts like **fixed wake time, morning light, and evening light restriction** can help that phenotype alongside CBT-I.

Best-practice habits for restless/disjointed sleep:

1. Keep a **fixed wake time** every day, weekends included.
2. Use the bed **only for sleep**; if awake >~20 min, get up and return when sleepy (stimulus control).
3. Get **morning daylight**; dim lights and cut screens in a wind-down window.
4. Limit long/late **naps** and catch-up sleep.
5. If fragmented sleep persists beyond a few weeks, see a provider to rule out **sleep apnea** and start **CBT-I**.
